headline: Highest risk is medium: shared Dify datastore plus broad egress and runtime-injected MCP/hooks create prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can share state via the Dify server datastore and processes uploaded knowledge-base content; Agent B uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks plus browser/tool access. That creates a plausible default pathway where B’s outputs or files can influence A, and A’s stored content can be treated as instructions. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented.
conditions: IF B writes attacker-controlled text into shared files or MCP outputs that A later ingests
IF A treats uploaded knowledge-base content as trusted instructions
IF the orchestrator passes B-generated content into A without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of shared files into A
Add provenance tags to B outputs before A reads them
Restrict B MCP hooks to allowlisted commands
Review one sample A/B handoff for instruction-like content
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance filtering

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches knowledge-base content, conversation logs, and model/tool credentials; B touches project code, AGENTS.md, README.md, session history, and provider auth data. Both have broad network egress, so a shared workspace or copied artifacts could leak sensitive material across the pair. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so this is inferred and escalated for uncertainty.
conditions: IF A and B operate on the same workspace or synced datastore
IF either agent uploads file contents or logs to external model providers
IF provider auth data from B is copied into A-visible context
mitigations: Separate workspaces for A and B
Remove secrets from shared files before handoff
Turn off automatic file upload where possible
Check logs for cross-agent data references
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data boundaries

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; B can run browsers and spawn subprocesses, and both have broad network egress. Even without explicit git write access, overlapping write-like authority over shared files or mutable project state can cause conflicts in default multi-agent operation. Uncertainty about the shared target increases severity rather than lowering it.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or project checkout
IF B edits files while A writes generated artifacts
IF the orchestrator lacks locking or optimistic concurrency controls
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories to each agent
Serialize write operations manually
Pause one agent during the other’s file edits
Check for concurrent file modifications after each task
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is an orchestration platform that can emit tool-driven outputs, while B is a support-oriented agent with browser and MCP/tool actions. If B consumes A’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions or code changes. The profiles do not show verification gates, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text as a source of truth
IF A-produced facts are forwarded into B’s browser or MCP actions
IF no human or programmatic verification step exists between them
mitigations: Require B to cite source lines before acting
Insert a manual review step for A outputs
Limit A to drafting only, not final instructions
Spot-check one end-to-end task for hallucinated facts
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: A handles conversation logs, knowledge-base content, and provider/tool credentials; B handles session history, project code, and provider authentication data. The profiles show different data classes and no documented retention/residency alignment, so a compliance mismatch is plausible. Because no specific jurisdiction or certification mismatch is stated, medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either agent’s logs or session history
IF retention policies differ between A and B deployments
IF provider authentication data is processed by both without a shared DPA or policy
mitigations: Classify data before sending it to either agent
Avoid placing regulated data in logs or session history
Compare retention settings for both deployments
Document which provider credentials each agent may touch
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls
